By
 Christian Robles ,
Technology Reporter, Nextgov/FCW 
 By
 Christian Robles 
 | 
 November 20, 2026 05:23 PM ET
 The agency says its National Provider Directory project is the long-term solution to data accuracy issues in the Plan Finder.
 CMS
 Seniors can still use an online tool to check whether doctors are in network for private Medicare Advantage plans after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services debuted the feature last year with significant errors.
 CMS told lawmakers it fixed those errors in a March letter shared with Nextgov/FCW , but underlying data about whether doctors are in-network are still not fully accurate. Three health care advocacy groups shared ideas to ensure the data are accurate with Nextgov/FCW .
 Seniors enrolling in Medicare can pick between private Medicare Advantage plans or traditional Medicare during an annual open enrollment period running from Oct. 15 through Dec. 7. Seniors interested in private plans can use the online Medicare Plan Finder to compare options. 
 Seniors could see whether doctors are in a Medicare Advantage plan’s network beginning with last year’s open enrollment period. When the feature first launched, it showed duplicate doctor addresses and conflicting information indicating that doctors were simultaneously in- and out-of-network for a Medicare Advantage plan, The Washington Post reported .
 Congressional Democrats raised concerns about the episode with CMS.
 CMS told lawmakers the issue was resolved by Oct. 17, 2025, and that it stemmed from CMS’ Plan Finder team misinterpreting the behavior of third-party SunFire application programming interfaces, according to the letter that was shared with Nextgov/FCW . 
 Specifically, one section of the Plan Finder code checked data within a 50-mile radius, while another section checked in-network status without that 50-mile radius in place, according to the CMS letter to Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden of Oregon.
 But ensuring Plan Finder information about doctors is accurate remains difficult.
 Seniors should verify Plan Finder information with Medicare Advantage plans before they enroll in a plan if having a particular doctor in network is important to them, Jeannie Fuglesten Biniek, deputy director for the program on Medicare policy at KFF, said in an interview.
 Screenshot of dummy data that shows physicians listed as out-of-network for an Aetna Medicare Advantage plan.  
 CMS makes a similar recommendation in the Plan Finder, telling seniors to “check with your provider to make sure they’re in the plan’s network” before enrolling in a plan.
 These checks are important because “plan networks can change at any time. Providers with multiple office locations may be in network at one location and out of network at another,” CMS says in the Plan Finder.
 This year’s Plan Finder includes a beta feature listing whether specific medical facilities are in- or out-of-network. That feature includes a similar disclaimer as the one for individual doctors.
 A CMS spokesperson told Nextgov/FCW that its National Provider Directory is its long-term solution to data accuracy issues. 
 That modernization project seeks to build a universal source of truth for information about doctors and providers by stringing together a variety of public and private sector data. It’s currently in a “preview release,” and it’s unclear when it will be fully released or if it will include information from private plans.
 Increasing data accuracy  
 As CMS works on the National Provider Directory, a new law could give seniors using the Plan Finder access to more accurate information.
 Starting in 2028, Medicare Advantage plans must verify their provider directories at least every 90 days, and remove out-of-network providers from directories within five business days. 
 American Medical Association president Dr. Willie Underwood III told Nextgov/FCW that the law is an “important step” for ensuring provider data are accurate.
 “Medicare should require plans to use the information they already have to verify directory data before relying on physicians to confirm it,” he added, while noting that physicians do still have a role in keeping information up to date. 
 The American Hospital Association told Nextgov/FCW in a statement that maintaining accurate provider data is the responsibility of private plans.
 Private plans are responsible for ensuring that the provider directory information they provide CMS is accurate, the agency spokesperson said. 
 The spokesperson also noted existing regulations meant to keep data accurate, such as a requirement that Medicare Advantage plans update Plan Finder information within 30 days of becoming aware of a change. 
 But continued collaboration between CMS, providers and health plans is what will ensure seniors have access to correct data through the Plan Finder, according to Chris Bond, a spokesperson for health plan trade group AHIP.
